node.label: Jeremy Black
node.date_label: The English Press in the Eighteenth Century (1987) · A Military Revolution? (1991) · Rethinking Military History (2004) · The British Seaborne Empire (2004)
node.description: A historian of warfare, British politics and the uses of history. The existing participant-editor reading of the military-revolution debate places him among critics of its conventional chronology, emphasizing continuity and later change. In his own written Sonshi interview he describes a comparative military history that challenges a restricted Western frame and resists a rigid separation between strategy and policy. Both arguments are scoped: the first is mediated by Clifford J. Rogers, the second is Black’s self-description, and neither establishes a single settled explanation of global military change.
node.representative_figures_and_works: The English Press in the Eighteenth Century (1987); A Military Revolution? Military Change and European Society 1550–1800 (1991); Rethinking Military History (2004); The British Seaborne Empire (2004).
node.scope_note: Existing jeremy_black identity and military roster context reused; old roster prose and source note remain exact. New global relation uses own written testimony. Rogers’s participant-editor mediation remains explicit, with no fresh reading of Black’s book or other anthology essays. No namesake union or causal Sun Tzu influence claim.

incident_edges.relationship: Questions conventional military-revolution chronology by emphasizing continuities and changes beyond its customary periodization.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Existing Rogers participant-editor introduction pp. 1–10 supplies the mediated debate characterization. Other essays and Black’s monograph are not newly read; earlier Western-expansion and theoretical-merit qualifications remain intact.

incident_edges.relationship: Challenges a restricted Western frame in military history and strategy through wider comparative context.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Own written answers on world history, China/India, strategy and diplomacy read. This is his stated methodological agenda, not verification of every book, a universal explanation or a Sun Tzu influence arrow.

named_group_routes.relationship: Nell recovers Black military service from patriotic exclusion
named_group_routes.evidence_note: His 1855 preface states this recovery project and credits Whittier’s compilation. This is a substantive contribution, not demonstrated reception by every later military historian.

named_group_routes.relationship: Brown uses collective biography to contest racist exclusion
named_group_routes.evidence_note: The 1863 preface explains this biographical project. Individual biographies and later reception remain unreviewed; the edge does not assert that Black history invented life writing.

named_group_routes.relationship: Black historiography’s independent roots test the limits of a later recovery umbrella
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Black history’s institutions and intellectual roots precede Hunt’s grouping; Gilroy also questions closed racial categories. This is a comparison of distinct projects, not an assertion of a single identity position or an influence event.

named_group_routes.relationship: shares diasporic and emancipatory arguments
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Diasporic and emancipatory concerns intersect, without making all Black and anti-colonial histories one school.

named_group_routes.relationship: Black women’s histories reshape analysis of race and gender
named_group_routes.evidence_note: White contributes a history of enslaved women; Higginbotham’s 1992 opening challenges thin racial analysis while developing feminist accounts of power. Distinct interventions, not a claim that one theorist founded intersectional inquiry.
named_group_routes.map_label: White and Higginbotham: race and gender

named_group_routes.relationship: centers enslaved people’s agency in the Haitian Revolution
named_group_routes.evidence_note: A contribution to anti-colonial historical writing, not merely a later recovery project under identity histories. The Black Jacobins makes enslaved revolutionaries historical agents; the argument is not supplied by a generic anti-colonial label.

named_group_routes.relationship: reworks Marxist history through Caribbean revolution and popular agency
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Connects distinct Marxist historical projects; does not make James a derivative of postwar British social history. James contributes a Caribbean revolutionary history within Marxist debate, not an example of all anti-colonial histories adopting one theory. The later lectures also reconsider the balance between prominent leaders and popular action. Hobsbawm’s participant memoir explicitly recalls the group reading The Black Jacobins across political differences.

named_group_routes.relationship: Caribbean historical writing and London Marxist study inform Rodney’s formation
named_group_routes.evidence_note: West’s assessment identifies The Black Jacobins. The Foundation names C. L. R. and Selma James in London study; James’s 1981 retrospective locates Rodney within a Caribbean intellectual inheritance. These sources support formation but not agreement on strategy or every textual debt.

named_group_routes.relationship: Cultural inquiry supplies resources for Gilroy’s Black Atlantic
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Gilroy’s preface names Hall among a wider range of resources and analyzes music and cultural movement. This is one explicit route, not the origin of all Atlantic history.
named_group_routes.map_label: Hall and cultural inquiry in Gilroy

named_group_routes.relationship: intersects and contends in interpretations of slavery, resistance, and power
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Black historians’ independent institutions and arguments are not treated as products of the New Left. Genovese’s preface acknowledges alternative national-culture readings; Johnson’s 2001 retrospective review contests consent/coercion in his account. This later assessment qualifies an earlier book without extending mapped coverage.

named_group_routes.relationship: Du Bois’s double consciousness enters Gilroy’s diaspora argument
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Gilroy explicitly identifies this conceptual resource in his preface. Porter Wesley’s Afro-Brazilian bibliography provides a separate material contribution to diaspora research; neither route makes the umbrella a single school.
named_group_routes.map_label: Du Bois and diaspora research resources

named_group_routes.relationship: places women’s rights organizing alongside labor and Black women’s activity before the 1960s
named_group_routes.evidence_note: James and Rupp identify broader coverage while offering different criticisms. Later women’s history is neither a uniform continuation nor a field founded by this book alone. Original 1959 text and later editions remain distinct.
named_group_routes.map_label: Rights organizing, labor and archival reach

named_group_routes.relationship: James’s later comparison takes up Du Bois on popular political imagination
named_group_routes.evidence_note: The 1971 lecture praises Black Reconstruction’s treatment of participants’ ideas. This is documented later engagement, not a claim that Du Bois supplied James’s original 1938 argument.

named_group_routes.relationship: Haitian revolution joins Caribbean and European revolutionary histories
named_group_routes.evidence_note: The Black Jacobins supplies an earlier regional contribution to later Atlantic inquiry. The edge marks subject and explanation, not proof that a single later Atlantic school descended from James.

named_group_routes.relationship: Feminist theories of power are resources for Higginbotham’s racial analysis
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Her 1992 opening credits conceptual advances and cites Scott, Butler and others while challenging their racial limits. This later exchange does not explain the origins of Black historiography.

named_group_routes.relationship: Black women’s archival participation exposes unequal authority and support within WCWA
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Voss-Hubbard pp. 20–21 reports Thurman/Bethune/NCNW involvement and dissatisfaction, with no Black directors and limited support for fieldwork. This criticism of organizational practice is mediated through the 1995 study, not a claim that all Black women shared one response or a direct refutation of the 1946 book.
named_group_routes.map_label: WCWA: racial inclusion, authority and resources

named_group_routes.relationship: Julie Richter identifies questions not asked about Black and Native women
named_group_routes.evidence_note: The 1999 review explicitly acknowledges their presence in the book while questioning the scope of inquiry; it also values regional/status distinctions and documents practical use. No total absence or dismissal of the book is asserted.
named_group_routes.map_label: Richter: racial scope of the inquiry

named_group_routes.relationship: Black historical collections and Terrell’s papers supply documentary resources for Flexner’s wider coverage
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Rupp p. 163 identifies Schomburg, Howard and Terrell collections in Flexner’s bibliography. This is mediated evidence of documentary use, not direct personal advice, consultation of those archives here or a claim that Black women’s activity was fully covered.
named_group_routes.map_label: Schomburg, Howard and Terrell documentary resources

named_group_routes.relationship: Rupp questions the limits of movement categories and the absence of private relationships in Flexner’s account
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Available 1992 passages value the inclusion of Black and white working women while questioning other exclusions and distinguishing historical self-identification from broader collective activity. Missing preview pages are not inferred; this is later reception.

named_group_routes.relationship: Frances James asks for a structural explanation through private property and a program beyond reform
named_group_routes.evidence_note: The 1960 review also welcomes labor and Black women’s coverage. This particular Marxist criticism does not make the book devoid of explanation, identify James with Janet Wilson James or establish a uniform Marxist response.

named_group_routes.relationship: Slavery scholarship and source collections provide resources for Genovese
named_group_routes.evidence_note: The preface and acknowledgments name Rawick, Levine and Litwack; permissions also identify Du Bois and Black historical source collections. This particular use respects Black history’s independent institutions and does not derive that field from the New Left.

named_group_routes.relationship: Massey uses Gilroy’s changing tradition as a resource
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Places and Their Pasts 184 explicitly invokes The Black Atlantic against a closed account of tradition. This is documented reception, not a new full-book check.

named_group_routes.relationship: Racial exclusion in urban institutions
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Sugrue’s Detroit history addresses racial inequality across work and housing; a shared problem does not establish descent from every Black historiographical tradition.

named_group_routes.relationship: Race, gender and historical explanation
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Higginbotham develops race as a metalanguage shaping gender, class and sexuality and as a contested instrument of power. Her opening programme combines feminist theory with Black intellectual traditions; no single undifferentiated school affiliation. The target is the named strand, displayed under its parent entry.

named_group_routes.relationship: African-Canadian historiography
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Walker's 1997 essay (full text read) identifies five orientations in African-Canadian historiography by the role assigned to Black people, ties the Community turn to Black Power, Black pride and social history, and to 'the collective nature of the black struggle in North America'. Later Canadian work is published in and framed by Black diaspora history: Mathieu (abstract) connects Black migrants and porters to 'black diaspora history during the Jim Crow era'; Austin publishes in the Journal of African American History (2007, metadata). Moved here from Immigration, ethnicity & race in Canada. The atlas entry's own scope note warns that diaspora links do not make Black histories one national tradition: this is a contribution, not a sub-field.

named_group_routes.relationship: Black migration and racialized immigration control
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Calliste (abstract read) shows immigration officials restricting Black Caribbean settlers while employers recruited their labour, 1900–32; Shepard (via Walker 1997) studies African American migration from Oklahoma to the prairies before 1914 and, by its subtitle, the racism the migrants met; Mathieu (abstract) joins immigration and Black diaspora history. Black Canadian history is not a sub-field of immigration history: of 177 PhDs citing Black Canadian history works, 45% engage Immigration, ethnicity & race in Canada (lift 3.4; 39% and lift 3.0 on a narrower definition). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence; lifts are high for most Canadian pairs.

named_group_routes.relationship: Black Montreal in the long 1960s
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Austin's Fear of a Black Nation (description read) centres the 1968 Congress of Black Writers and the Black-led protest at Sir George Williams University; Forsythe's 1971 collection is a contemporary participants' account, not scholarship; Austin 2007 is title-level. All selected scholarship is post-2000, so this comparison rests on later work; Canada’s 1960s declined a black – Canada’s 1960s edge for the same reason, and this edge is the narrower Canadian pair. PhD context: 40% of PhDs citing Black Canadian history works engage Canada’s 1960s (lift 2.8).

named_group_routes.relationship: Slavery in New France and Black Quebec
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Trudel, a Laval historian of New France on the Quebec roster, wrote the francophone history of slavery in French Canada (1960, checked against Hamelin's RHAF review heading) and its dictionary (1990, which Walker 1997 lists among works on slavery); Gay (2004) and the French edition of Mackey (2013) continue a francophone strand, and Mackey is read mostly at francophone universities (5 of 9 PhDs). Bibliographic level only; no checked text frames the two literatures against each other. PhD context: 16 of 177 PhDs citing Black Canadian history works are at francophone universities; 37% engage Quebec historiography (lift 2.3).

named_group_routes.relationship: African Canadian women's history
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Walker (1997, full text) notes that 'black women have been receiving increasing attention' and uses Brand's No Burden to Carry as his example of the Survivors orientation; We're Rooted Here (1994) is a six-author volume of African Canadian women's history; Bonner's review (read) calls Flynn's Moving Beyond Borders a contribution to 'a sparse literature relative to the lives of African Canadian women'. PhD context: 61% of PhDs citing Black Canadian history works engage Canadian women's & gender history (lift 2.4).

named_group_routes.relationship: Black workers, porters and segmented labour
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Calliste (1987, title-level) treats Black sleeping car porters as an 'ethnically submerged split labour market'; Mathieu (abstract read) follows porters and their union, white railwaymen's demands for a segregated workforce, and porters as civil-rights leaders. PhD context: 48% of PhDs citing Black Canadian history works engage Canadian working-class history (lift 2.2). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

named_group_routes.relationship: Black soldiers and race in recruitment
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Walker's 'Race and Recruitment in World War I' (CHR 1989, metadata) is the scholarly study of visible-minority enlistment in the CEF that Canadian military history also uses, and Ruck's Black Battalion (1987) is a community history of the No. 2 Construction Battalion; Walker 1997 lists both in his reading for African-Canadian history. Title-level only. PhD context: 17% of PhDs citing Black Canadian history works engage Canadian military history (lift 1.2), so this is a narrow shared subject, not a shared readership.

named_group_routes.relationship: Antimodernism and the invented folk in twentieth-century Nova Scotia (1992, 1994)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: In-period evidence (1992, 1994). In 'Tartanism Triumphant' (Acadiensis, 1992; pp. 5–9 read) McKay asks how Nova Scotia 'became Scottish' in the second quarter of the twentieth century, when 'a collection of hazy generalizations and ethnic stereotypes' became 'a natural and obvious "commonsense"'. His broad answer: 'it was part of an international anti-modernist wave, a local version of a general middle-class search for something outside and better than the crisis-ridden modern world it inhabited' (pp. 8–9); the narrow answer is the state's cultural power under Angus L. Macdonald. Note 12 takes Lears's definition of American antimodernism and adds the 'simple life' and 'nature'. The Quest of the Folk (1994) is checked at summary and contents level: chapters on 'The Idea of the Folk', Helen Creighton and folklore, Mary Black and handicrafts, the simple life, and the folk 'under conditions of postmodernity'. Muise's review essay (Acadiensis, 1998; pp. 128–32 read) describes the three case studies and quotes the book's conclusion that 'the concept of the Folk was and remains a powerful obstacle to the formation of a counter-hegemonic cultural politics' (p. 306). Wright's 1995 Acadiensis review essay on English-Canadian intellectual history cites the book for 'a very skilled handling of Antonio Gramsci's theory of cultural hegemony by an historian' (p. 132 n. 29). A contribution to the field's cultural strand, not its origin: Berger, McKillop and Owram precede it. In the sampled corpus, 56 of 1,303 strict History doctoral dissertations dated 2009–2026 cite the book. Bibliographies record consultation, not influence. In the Province of History (2010, with Bates) is a later reading.

named_group_routes.relationship: Culture and Imperialism's account of resistance culture: anticolonial histories such as James's The Black Jacobins and Antonius's The Arab Awakening read as a 'voyage in' to metropolitan culture, alongside post-independence critiques by Guha and Alatas (1993)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: His own in-period text. Culture and Imperialism (Knopf, 1993), chapter 3, 'Resistance and Opposition'. He distinguishes liberal anti-colonialism, which did 'not dispute the fundamental superiority of Western man', from anti-imperialism, and argues 'there was no overall condemnation of imperialism until—and this is my point—after native uprisings were too far gone to be ignored or defeated' (pp. 240–241). Anti-imperialist work by writers from the peripheries in the metropolis is 'usually an extension into the metropolis of large-scale mass movements'; 'There is thus an overlap and interdependence that cannot theoretically be described as only the reactive assertion of a separate colonial or native identity'; 'The voyage in, then, constitutes an especially interesting variety of hybrid cultural work' (p. 244). He reads 'C.L.R. James's The Black Jacobins, published in 1938, and, appearing at almost the same time, George Antonius's The Arab Awakening' as works 'intended as serious works of scholarship and advocacy addressed from within a national movement for independence to a general audience', set against Ranajit Guha's A Rule of Property for Bengal (1963) and S. H. Alatas's The Myth of the Lazy Native (1977), which are 'post-colonial and specialist' (p. 245); 'history for Guha is critique, not the dutiful replication of colonialist objects, ideologies, and arguments' (p. 251). He also treats Fanon as one who 'programmatically seeks to treat colonial and metropolitan societies together' (p. 278). The introduction frames the chapter: 'What I left out of Orientalism was that response to Western dominance which culminated in the great movement of decolonization' (p. xii). Read: pp. xii, 240–245, 251, 278; the rest of the chapter (including the Fanon and Cabral sections) was not read closely. No in-period review assessing this chapter for historians was read. A contribution to how anticolonial histories are read and placed, not a claim that he wrote anticolonial history in their sense; The Question of Palestine (1979) is mentioned in the node, not used for this edge.
named_group_routes.map_label: Resistance culture and the voyage in, 1993

named_group_routes.relationship: Williams’s Capitalism and Slavery tested on the compensation records: supported on slave-wealth in British society, qualified on decline, and set against a British Marxist pantheon that left James and Williams out (2009–2014)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own words, read (History Workshop Journal 78, 2014). "C. L. R James and Eric Williams did not appear in their pantheon. James and Williams, in their struggle against racism and colonialism insisted on the linkage between metropole and colony … the intimate connections … between capitalism and slavery" (p. 23). "Williams never argued that slavery 'caused' the Industrial Revolution … as Nicholas Draper, Keith McClelland and I suggest in the co-authored book which documents the results of the first phase of our project on the Legacies of British Slave-Ownership (LBS), there is a move to a modified version of Williams’s thesis amongst economic historians" (p. 24); "Williams’s insight into the importance of slave-derived wealth to eighteenth-century society and culture has been greatly expanded" (p. 24). Qualifications: the modified thesis is attributed jointly to the LBS authors and set among economic historians (Pomeranz, Inikori); it is not a claim that slavery caused industrialization. The jointly written introduction to Legacies of British Slave-ownership (2014; read in part by the second research pass, without print pages) tests Williams directly: "Eric Williams' Capitalism and Slavery included four connected arguments that are critical for us"; "our findings are entirely supportive of Williams in the context of this second thesis" (slave-wealth in British society); on industrialisation "Our material cannot resolve these controversies"; and the work "complicates Williams by qualifying his 'decline' thesis". Katie Donington, a co-author, recalls that "The project foregrounded Williams's work" (Black Perspectives, 2020). Hall was the project's principal investigator (REF 2014 case study).

named_group_routes.relationship: The Black Jacobins as a model for analysing “metropole and colony in one lens” (2003)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own acknowledgement, read by the second research pass (JBS 42:4, 2003, p. 533): "Colonizers were made both in the metropole and on colonial sites. And, as C. L. R. James's The Black Jacobins (1938) taught us, much can be gained through the analysis of metropole and colony in one lens." A retrospective acknowledgement made in defending the book's method; it names a resource, not the origin of her project. Her 2014 essay also sets James and Williams against the British Marxist pantheon (History Workshop Journal 78, p. 23, read).
named_group_routes.map_label: Metropole and colony in one lens, 2003

named_group_routes.relationship: The Age of… volumes (1962–1994) as a synthesis of “the capitalist world from 1789 to 1991”, praised by reviewers for range and analytical grasp and called “unashamedly Eurocentric” by Judt
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Mediated: the four volumes are unread. Guardian obituarists (2012, read in full): the series "distilled the history of the capitalist world from 1789 to 1991" and "were not conceived as a tetralogy". Judt (NYRB 1995, read in full): the trilogy's scheme "eventually became the “conventional” interpretation, now exposed to steady criticism and revision"; "though unashamedly Eurocentric, Eric Hobsbawm has a unique range" (his endnote 2 defends the European focus). Black (Historein 2003–4, p. 215): "authoritative and commanding overviews of international history from the 18th century to present". Anderson (LRB 2002) quotes Hobsbawm on Interesting Times as "world history shaping that experience". At the 2014 conference (Times Higher Education report) Mazower spoke of a "golden age of historical synthesis". Counterweights: Judt's Eurocentrism remark and the existing critiques by Guha and Chakrabarty (edges 979, 917).
named_group_routes.map_label: The Age of… synthesis, 1962–94, per reviewers

named_group_routes.relationship: Industrial Britain and its workers: the standard-of-living debate of the 1950s and Industry and Empire (1968), which his readers credit with recasting the economic history of Britain
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Mediated: no economic-history text by Hobsbawm was read (his 1957 Economic History Review article is metadata only). Judt (NYRB 1995): Labouring Men, Industry and Empire and Captain Swing "substantially recast the economic history of Britain and the story of the British labor movement"; Hobsbawm is "by training and inclination an economic historian, and an analytical one at that". Guardian obituarists (2012): the "once celebrated 'standard of living' debate", in which he and R. M. Hartwell "traded arguments in successive numbers of the Economic History Review", and Industry and Empire (1968) as "a compelling summation of much of his work on Britain and the industrial revolution". Black (Historein, p. 215): "a key protagonist in the standard of living in the industrial revolution debates … something of a Cold War battleground". A pre-2000 gap repair; not a claim about the transition debate.
named_group_routes.map_label: Standard of living and Industry and Empire, per readers

named_group_routes.relationship: Hartman's 'critical fabulation' and Fuentes's black-feminist reading of 'fragmentary sources' (2016) take the archive's violence as the problem of Black history
named_group_routes.evidence_note: MacArthur's description (read); Fuentes's publisher description (read). The black entry's strand archives ('Collecting and diaspora bibliography') is the hook. Trouillot's clause was removed after review (finding 9): p4A_rel_25 carries it.
named_group_routes.map_label: The violence of the archive in Black history, 2008–16

named_group_routes.relationship: Silencing the Past 'remains an unavoidable reference for anyone navigating the streams of Black and Caribbean studies in academia and beyond' (Craipain, 2024); Bulamah, Goyatá and Pereira read 'The Odd and the Ordinary' as challenging an exceptionalist image that isolates Haiti from its surrounding world (2020, paragraph 5)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Craipain 2024 (read in full); Bulamah et al. 2020, paras 3–5 (read). Corrected after review (finding 7): the phrase 'dominated by Christianity, capitalism, and whiteness' (1990a: 7) describes the surrounding world, not Haiti's exceptionalist image, and is no longer quoted here.
named_group_routes.map_label: Haiti in Black and Caribbean studies, 1990–2024

named_group_routes.relationship: Race as the outcome of 'differentiation, which is an intensely conflictual process' (2001): 'a race cannot be taken as given. It is made in the targeting'; Black people 'racialized as slaves', Indians eliminated 'as Indians' (2006); a comparative typology of colonial race regimes in Traces of History (2016)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Wolfe 2006 (read in full), opening section: "different racial regimes encode and reproduce the unequal relationships into which Europeans coerced the populations concerned"; "Black people's enslavement produced an inclusive taxonomy … For Indians, in stark contrast, non-Indian ancestry compromised their indigeneity"; "a race cannot be taken as given. It is made in the targeting"; and note 62 quoting his own 2001 essay, p. 894: "Difference … is not simply given. It is the outcome of differentiation, which is an intensely conflictual process." The 2001 essay is otherwise unread (Crossref: AHR 106:3, June 2001). Traces of History (2016) known through the British Library contents note (chapters on Australia, the United States, central Europe, Brazil, Palestine) and Veracini's obituary (read): it "utilises his analysis of racism under settler colonialism in order to explain racism everywhere else" and provides "a compelling typology of racial formations". Strengthens the entry-level comparison edge_885, which stays. (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

named_group_routes.relationship: Black Reconstruction (1935) reinterprets emancipation and Reconstruction through Black agency and an interrupted experiment in multiracial democracy, as Chad Williams reads it (2022).
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Williams’s introduction, read, supplies this characterization; the full 1935 book is not newly read. The existing field roster is retained, and this contribution does not claim sole founding of Black historical scholarship.

named_group_routes.relationship: The Philadelphia Negro (1899) examines a specific Black urban community; Elijah Anderson’s 2023 introduction emphasizes employment discrimination and the limits of expecting reform from informed employers.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: A named reader’s interpretation of the 1899 Philadelphia survey. This is a contribution through one study, not a claim that Du Bois founded all urban history. Isabel Eaton’s domestic-service study is separately credited; it is not treated as Du Bois’s sole-authored research.

named_group_routes.relationship: Independent historical research and publishing: antebellum education (1915), the Journal of Negro History (1916), migration history (1918), and a critique of educational dependence (1933).
named_group_routes.evidence_note: The 1919 education preface, 1918 migration preface/opening, and 1933 preface/chapter I were read. Pyne and the NPS supply institutional dates. Earlier Black historical organizations and community support preclude a sole-founder claim.

named_group_routes.relationship: Negro History Week (1926) combines public historical education with the research and publishing programme supported by Black communities.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Pyne’s LOC essay describes the programme and community financing; the NPS reproduces Woodson’s public-education statement. This is a documented commemorative/educational practice predating the later professional label public history, not self-identification with that profession or sole invention of commemoration.

named_group_routes.relationship: The culture of dissemblance: sexual violence, privacy and Black women’s migration require analytical explanation beyond the recovery of prominent lives (1989).
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own essay, pp.912–916 and 919–920 read. Hine treats sexual/personal motives as additions to economic explanations and acknowledges that dissemblance can be mistaken for control over hostile representations. Her historical generalizations are not universal findings for all Black women.

named_group_routes.relationship: Black Women in White (1989) studies Black nurses’ struggles against racial and gender exclusion; Hine’s later argument makes parallel professional organizations important to resistance (2003).
named_group_routes.evidence_note: The nursing-book interpretation is attributed to Celia J. Wintz’s read repository abstract; the book is not newly read. Hine’s 2003 published opening extract, rather than the whole address, supplies the parallel-institutions argument. A scoped contribution to nursing/professional history, not founding medical history.

named_group_routes.relationship: Critical fabulation confronts the violence of slavery’s archive while requiring narrative restraint and acknowledging the failure to recover the dead (2008).
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Hartman’s pp.9 and 11–14, read. She distinguishes speculation from verified recovery and refuses closure; no claim that invention supplies lost testimony is accepted. This personal methodological contribution is different from the existing aggregate archive-to-Atlantic and archive-to-Black-history arrows.

named_group_routes.relationship: Wayward Lives (2019) places ordinary young Black women’s experiments in living at the center of historical explanation, while refusing to reproduce state case files’ pathologizing judgments.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: The book’s method is read through Hartman’s 2020 first-person interviews and the 2019 institutional account, not a new whole-book reading. This contribution concerns women’s history and its subjects; the generic archive/Atlantic relationships are retained separately.

named_group_routes.relationship: Hartman admires Du Bois’s intellectual achievement but criticizes the Philadelphia survey’s elite and Victorian judgments about Black intimate life (2020 interview).
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Explicit first-person answer to Yannise Jean about Du Bois, read. The criticism is dated to the 2020 interview and limited to these class/gender judgments, rather than a wholesale rejection of Du Bois or a passage independently checked in the 2019 book.

named_group_routes.relationship: With Deborah Gray White and a collective of researchers, Scarlet and Black (2016) brings Rutgers’s involvement in slavery and dispossession into the university’s public history.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Publisher description and contents, read, establish a jointly edited committee publication with separately named chapter authors. White wrote its introduction; Fuentes is neither sole author nor sole discoverer. verification.note: Complete text and endnotes read for revision 1.147 (NYRB page; no pagination). A "Hobsbawm generation" of historians who began between about 1959 and 1975; Primitive Rebels "first appeared in 1959"; Labouring Men, Industry and Empire and Captain Swing "substantially recast the economic history of Britain and the story of the British labor movement"; the trilogy's scheme "eventually became the “conventional” interpretation"; The Age of Revolution 1962, The Age of Capital 1975 ("Hobsbawm’s single greatest work"), The Age of Empire twelve years later. Hobsbawm is "by training and inclination an economic historian, and an analytical one" who "mostly avoids military or political narrative"; "though unashamedly Eurocentric, Eric Hobsbawm has a unique range" (endnote 2 defends the European focus). The "one" defect: "the categories right/left, fascist/Communist, progressive and reactionary seem to be very firmly set, and pretty much as they first presented themselves to Hobsbawm in the Thirties"; Bolshevism gets "no critical analytical attention except on its own restricted terms"; "“real socialism” in the lands between Germany and Russia merits just six pages"; nationalism "is a rather neglected subject". Verdict: "a challenging, often brilliant, and always cool and intelligent account". The Age of Extremes itself is unread.
